strengths: Sound theoretical framework with rigorous Wasserstein stability analysis (Prop. 2.3) and characterization of optimal rank-r reconstruction (Prop. 4.1) for both stochastic and deterministic operator learning

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse benchmarks (stochastic Burgers, Darcy, KS, Kolmogorov) with rich metrics including distributional (ED, SWD), moment-based (NRMSEm, NRMSEs), and calibration (CRPS, SSR) measures

Architecture-agnostic design preserving discretization invariance and geometry handling of backbone operators; unified framework handling both stochastic (Problem 2.1) and deterministic (Problem 2.2) settings
Consistent improvements over baselines with particularly strong calibration results (SSR near 1); qualitative visualizations effectively demonstrate improved spatial structure capture
Excellent reproducibility documentation with extensive appendices detailing architectural choices, hyperparameters, dataset generation, and implementation details
weaknesses: Latent Diffusion (LDM) baseline shows surprisingly poor performance on rollout benchmarks (Table 5: CRPS=1.232 vs DLL=0.822; SSR=0.548 vs DLL=0.620) with no explanation or ablation study—raises concerns about implementation fairness or fundamental limitations not discussed

Critical ablations missing: (1) no sensitivity analysis on latent dimension r (fixed at 64); (2) no ablation isolating contribution of input-dependent basis Φ(a) vs. standard autoencoder; (3) unclear why operator encoder achieves worse stochastic reconstruction than AE (Table 6: 4.13e-2 vs 7.75e-4) yet still improves overall performance

Strong Assumptions A.11 (universal approximation) and A.4 (Lipschitz continuity in condition) are posited but never empirically verified on learned models; theoretical-practical gap between Proposition 2.3's Wasserstein bound (depends on potentially large Grönwall constant) and practical performance unclear

Computational cost analysis absent: no wall-clock time, FLOPs, or memory comparisons despite efficiency claims; iterative diffusion sampling overhead in coefficient space not quantified; fairness of comparing 64-dimensional coefficient predictions against full-resolution baselines questionable

Incremental novelty: operator encoder is standard conditional autoencoder with input-dependent basis; diffusion component uses standard flow matching; main contribution combines existing techniques rather than introducing fundamentally new methods or insights

strengths: Addresses a practical problem of uncertainty quantification for neural operators with clear motivation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (stochastic PDEs, chaotic rollouts) with diverse metrics
Solid theoretical grounding with Wasserstein stability analysis (Proposition 2.3) and characterization of optimal encoder solutions (Proposition 4.1)
Unified framework handles both stochastic and deterministic settings within one approach
Extensive appendices provide implementation details, proofs, and dataset generation information
Clear presentation with informative figures and reasonable exposition overall
weaknesses: Limited novelty: combines well-established components (latent diffusion, operator encoders, flow matching) without significant new insights. Missing ablation studies make it impossible to identify which components drive improvements

Inconsistent experimental improvements: DLL is not uniformly better than baselines; notably underperforms pixel-space diffusion on Kolmogorov flow (Table 5: DLL 0.426 vs DM 0.369). Other improvements are marginal (3-6%) and lack statistical significance testing (no error bars, single runs)

Unjustified critical design choices: latent dimension r=64 used throughout without justification or ablation study despite being crucial to the bottleneck. Two-stage training (freeze encoder after stage 1) not compared to joint training. MLP denoiser not motivated

Theory-experiment disconnect: Proposition 2.3's Wasserstein bound involves unspecified Grönwall constants with unclear practical implications and is never empirically validated. Proposition 4.1 requires unrealistic universal approximation assumption (A.11) never verified empirically. Tables 6-7 show encoder fails to recover claimed KL structure well on stochastic problems

Contradicts main claim of 'architecture agnostic' approach: all experiments use FNO backbone exclusively; no tests with DeepONet, U-NO, or other neural operator architectures despite being mentioned in related work

Reconstruction property paradox (Tables 6-7): operator encoder achieves lower error on deterministic benchmarks despite higher compression, yet higher error on stochastic problems. Suggests input-dependent basis may not be the key driver. Inconsistency unexplained

Questionable epistemic uncertainty interpretation: Section 3.3 claims underfitting connects to epistemic uncertainty because L_V remains nonzero, but this connection is informal and lacks rigor. Could simply reflect optimization failure. Needs formalization or removal

Missing critical ablations: no sensitivity analysis on latent dimension r; no comparison of joint vs. two-stage training; no different baseline diffusion variants (score vs. flow); no experiments with multiple seeds or statistical significance testing

strengths: Solid theoretical framework with rigorous proofs connecting velocity matching to Wasserstein distance (Prop. 2.3) and showing optimal rank-r KL reconstruction (Prop. 4.1)
Architecture-agnostic design that preserves discretization invariance while enabling efficient sampling in low-dimensional coefficient space
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse benchmarks (stochastic and chaotic systems) with complementary metrics and detailed implementation details
Clear and well-organized presentation with informative figures and thorough appendices supporting reproducibility
Unified framework for both stochastic (aleatoric) and deterministic (epistemic) uncertainty quantification
weaknesses: Empirical improvements are often modest and inconsistent: stochastic benchmarks show small margins over LDM/DM (Tables 2-3), and deterministic rollouts show mixed results with DLL underperforming on Kolmogorov flow (NRMSE 0.426 vs DM 0.369 in Table 5)
Critical missing ablations: no study of encoder fine-tuning, sensitivity to latent dimension r (fixed at 64 across all problems), or how reconstruction error propagates to final performance

Reconstruction analysis (Section 5.4) is disconnected from main narrative and incompletely justified—operator encoder underperforms standard autoencoders on stochastic problems without clear explanation

Limited novelty: straightforward combination of existing techniques (operator encoders + diffusion models), with theoretical contributions primarily applying existing frameworks rather than developing fundamentally new theory
Incomplete experimental scope: only FNO backbone tested despite claiming architecture-agnosticism, all benchmarks on regular grids, no real-world applications, and only 4 benchmarks total
Theoretical gaps: tightness of Wasserstein bounds unexplored, Assumption A.4 (Lipschitz continuity) assumed but not verified for trained models, no sample complexity analysis
Parameter efficiency claims are contradicted by Table 9 showing DLL using more parameters in 2D (17.944M vs 9.743M for LDM)
Hyperparameter choices (T=10, r=64) lack justification or sensitivity analysis, and no computational cost comparisons with baselines

strengths: Well-motivated modular architecture combining neural operators with conditional diffusion in low-dimensional coefficient space, enabling computational efficiency
Sound theoretical framework with rigorous proofs connecting velocity matching loss to Wasserstein distance (Prop 2.3) and characterizing optimal rank-r reconstruction (Prop 4.1)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning stochastic (Burgers, Darcy) and deterministic (KS, Kolmogorov) benchmarks with extensive ablations on rank, NFE, dataset size, and backbone compatibility
Strong qualitative results demonstrating DLL captures spatially structured uncertainty better than baselines, with improved rollout stability and informative uncertainty bands
Clear presentation with rigorous mathematics, effective visualizations, and extensive appendices; modular design compatible with multiple operator backbones (FNO, DeepONet)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: combines well-established components (neural operators, latent diffusion) with operator-inspired basis; theoretical contributions largely apply existing stability results rather than developing new theory
Modest empirical improvements: gains often 10-20% (e.g., Stochastic Darcy: 0.227 vs 0.269), inconsistent across problems (DM outperforms DLL on Kolmogorov deterministic NRMSE 0.369 vs 0.426)

Uncertainty quantification claims overstated: deterministic-setting uncertainty relies on heuristic 'diffusion underfitting' (residual variance in L_V), not principled or calibrated; Proposition A.4 only guarantees W₂ continuity, not calibration guarantees
Reconstruction property asymmetry unexplained: standard autoencoders outperform operator encoders on stochastic benchmarks (Table 6-7), contradicting core motivation for input-dependent bases

Limited experimental scope: only standard well-behaved PDEs, small test sets (32 samples), no high-dimensional or multiscale problems; no wall-clock time analysis despite two-stage training complexity
Incomplete justification for design choices: non-monotonic ablation on rank (r=64 not clearly optimal), architecture selections lack justification, sensitivity unexplored
Limited failure mode analysis: explanation for underperformance on Kolmogorov is vague ('ceiling depends on backbone'); robustness to weaker operators unexplored

strengths: Well-motivated operator encoder design with solid theoretical connection to optimal rank-r Karhunen-Loève reconstruction (Proposition 4.1)
Modular architecture compatible with different neural operator backbones (FNO, DeepONet)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning both stochastic and deterministic systems with multiple metrics, ablations, and qualitative analysis
Clear presentation with extensive appendices providing implementation details and additional results
Addresses a genuine need for computationally efficient uncertainty quantification in neural operators
weaknesses: Limited novelty—primarily combines three established components (neural operators, latent diffusion, learned bases) without fundamental methodological innovation

Mixed experimental results with modest improvements: on Darcy DLL ties with baselines on SWD; on Kolmogorov flow DM outperforms DLL on NRMSE (0.369 vs 0.426); authors acknowledge diffusion may be superior for complex dynamics

Unvalidated uncertainty quantification claims: no calibration metrics, coverage guarantees, or comparison to Bayesian methods; admission that 'extending such guarantees to DLL is important future work'
Paradoxical design choice: operator encoder (OE) underperforms autoencoder (AE) on stochastic benchmarks (Tables 6-7), yet DLL somehow works—this contradiction receives insufficient investigation
Non-monotonic ablations (Table 10-11) showing better reconstruction does NOT correlate with better distributional fidelity, suggesting poorly understood optimization dynamics

Unfair experimental comparisons: baselines (DM/LDM) use U-Nets while DLL uses FNO; parameter counts differ by 10-15× (Table 8-9), making it unclear whether improvements stem from method or architecture

Weak theoretical contributions: Proposition 2.3 follows straightforwardly from standard continuity equation stability; Proposition 4.1 is somewhat expected given MSE loss; Proposition A.4 is basic regularity
Limited scope: only regular grids (except one DeepONet experiment), small test sets (32-128 samples), no real-world applications, restricted to simple benchmark problems
Two-stage encoder-then-diffusion training lacks justification; no end-to-end training comparison despite this potentially being suboptimal
Missing statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing despite small test sets; incomplete code availability limits reproducibility

strengths: Well-motivated and elegant approach that combines neural operators with diffusion in a principled way, preserving discretization invariance while enabling efficient probabilistic modeling
Strong theoretical contributions: Proposition 2.3 connects velocity matching to Wasserstein distance with rigorous proofs; Proposition 4.1 establishes recovery of optimal rank-r KL expansions

Comprehensive experimental evaluation covering stochastic PDEs, deterministic long-horizon rollouts, multiple baselines, and extensive ablations; results demonstrate clear improvements in capturing spatial structure of uncertainty

Practical advantages including modularity (works with any backbone), parameter efficiency compared to autoencoders, efficient sampling in coefficient space, and demonstrated compatibility with different architectures

Rigorous presentation with clear problem formulation, complete proofs, detailed experimental protocols, and transparent discussion of limitations; high reproducibility with implementation details and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: combines existing techniques (operator encoders, latent diffusion) in a useful but incremental way; primarily an engineering contribution rather than fundamental innovation

Inconsistent empirical improvements: pixel-space diffusion outperforms DLL on Kolmogorov flow (NRMSE 0.369 vs 0.426, CRPS 0.692 vs 0.822); performance heavily dependent on backbone quality; method trades mean accuracy for uncertainty quantification

Operator encoder design underjustified: Assumption A.11 (universal approximation) is strong but never empirically validated; reconstruction can be worse than autoencoders on stochastic problems (Tables 6-7); no principled method for choosing rank r (ablations show non-monotonic behavior)

Uncertainty quantification claims lack rigor: Section 3.3 claims diffusion underfitting indicates epistemic uncertainty in deterministic settings but this is heuristic without calibration guarantees; authors acknowledge this is not a true epistemic uncertainty guarantee but use it anyway

Scalability and scope limitations: experiments restricted to small grids (256×256 max), regular domains only, synthetic benchmarks only; no real-world evaluation; two-stage training adds complexity; no computational cost comparisons provided

Parameter count fairness issues: DM/LDM are 5-8× larger than FNO methods (Table 8); unclear if their better performance reflects architectural advantages or capacity advantage; DLL encoder can exceed autoencoder size in 2D (Table 9)

Reconstruction quality degradation on stochastic problems not adequately addressed: Tables 6-7 show operator encoder reconstruction substantially worse than autoencoders, directly impacting downstream diffusion quality but minimally discussed

Missing empirical analysis: no failure mode discussion, no discretization invariance validation, minimal exploration of sensitivity to encoder training quality, no investigation of why r=64 is optimal despite non-monotonic ablations
